Karmayoga, "the yoga of action," takes up the question Arjuna presses at the outset: if wisdom is better than action, as chapter 2 seemed to say, why does Kṛṣṇa still urge him to fight? Kṛṣṇa answers by denying the premise — no one can remain without acting even for a moment, since everyone is driven to act by the guṇas of nature (verses 4-8) — and then reframes what action itself can be. The middle of the chapter reads the old Vedic cycle of sacrifice as a figure for unattached action: gods and men sustain one another through yajña, and the chain of dependence traced from rain to food to beings is grounded, at last, in brahman itself (verses 9-16). Kṛṣṇa then holds up the free man, exemplified by the philosopher-king Janaka and by Kṛṣṇa's own case, who acts with nothing left to gain, solely for loka-saṃgraha, "the world's welfare" — and asks Arjuna to act the same way, without unsettling those who still cling to the fruits of their own work (verses 17-29). The chapter's second half turns to the real obstacle to such freedom: not action itself but kāma, desire, which wears the mask of anger and covers wisdom the way smoke covers fire, dust a mirror, or a caul an unborn child (verses 36-39). Its remedy is a discipline of hierarchy — senses, mind, understanding, and beyond all of these the self — mastered by force of that highest self, with which the chapter closes.
